meta.title: Rebranding for SMEs: 7 signs it's time | Renee
meta.description: When is a rebrand worth it? Seven clear signs, common mistakes and how Swiss SMEs can renew their brand without losing recognition.

title: Rebranding for SMEs: 7 signs your brand needs an update
author: Renee Studio
summary: Brands age quietly. The logo worked once, the colours suited the times, the website looked modern. Then the business grows, the offer changes, and suddenly your brand is telling a story that no longer fits. Here is how to tell when an update is due, and how to approach it without putting your customers' trust at risk.

p: Not every change is a full rebrand. A **refresh** modernises existing elements: typeface, colours, imagery, a polished logo. A **rebrand** goes deeper and touches positioning, name, messaging and sometimes the entire identity. For most SMEs, a targeted refresh is the right first step.

sections.h: 7 signs your brand needs an update

sub.h: 1. Your offer has changed, your brand hasn't
p: You have new services, new target groups or a new market, but your logo, tagline and website still speak the language of ten years ago.

sub.h: 2. Your brand looks different on every channel
p: Website, quotes, social media and vehicle livery look as if they came from different companies. A lack of consistency costs recognition, and with it trust.
Too thin, too detailed, illegible as a favicon or profile picture. A modern logo has to work at 32 pixels just as well as on a trade-fair wall.

sub.h: 4. You constantly have to explain what you actually do
p: If prospects need to ask after the first contact what exactly you offer, your brand isn't conveying your positioning.

sub.h: 5. Your competitors look more professional, even though you're better
p: Customers compare in seconds. An outdated look makes even strong work seem smaller.

sub.h: 6. You're not winning the customers you want
p: If most of your enquiries are price-driven, your brand may be sending the wrong signals.

sub.h: 7. Your team isn't proud of the brand
p: When employees are reluctant to hand out business cards or would rather not mention the website in conversation, that is an honest warning sign.

sections.h: How to approach a rebrand in a structured way
list: **Take stock:** What works today? What do customers recognise? Keep these elements on purpose.
**Sharpen your positioning:** Who are you for, what sets you apart, what do you promise? Only then does design begin.
**Develop a visual system:** Logo, colours, typography, imagery and layout grid as one system, not as separate parts.
**Prioritise applications:** Start with the touchpoints that have the greatest impact: website, quote templates, social media profiles.
**Roll it out properly:** A short brand manual and ready-made templates keep the new look consistent in everyday use.
Changing everything at once and losing recognition in the process
Renewing only the logo and forgetting the website and templates
Designing before the positioning is clear
No brand manual, so things drift apart again after three months

p: A good rebrand feels familiar to existing customers and wins over new audiences at first glance. What matters is not the size of the change, but that brand and business tell the same story again.

faq.q: How much does a rebrand cost for an SME?
faq.a: It depends on the scope. A refresh with a reworked logo, colour and type system costs considerably less than a complete repositioning. You can find our starting prices on the [pricing page](@pricing).

faq.q: How long does a rebrand take?
faq.a: A refresh typically takes a few weeks; a comprehensive rebrand including the website takes more like two to three months.

faq.q: Will we lose customers through a rebrand?
faq.a: Not if recognisable elements are carried over deliberately and the change is communicated actively.
